transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-28 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (Solis Head of ML), Marcus Li (Platform Eng), Rima Khan (CTO)

Summary / Auto notes: Jordan gave a short recap, Priya walked through the new bench dashboard, then we discussed a few tail latency spikes and a routing hypothesis. Action items captured at end.

[00:00] Jordan: Okay everybody can hear me? Great. Thanks for joining the Sprint 4 show and tell. We have about 55 minutes on the call, we wanted to walk through the numbers, highlight a couple of outliers, and propose a short dedicated-slot canary.

[00:22] Ellen: Yep, all good here. Appreciate the time. We've been excited to see some of the p50 wins you mentioned in Slack.

[00:30] Priya: Hi all, I will share my screen in a sec — apologies if the auto transcribe messes up names, it sometimes does. I uploaded the latest csvs into the bench sheet, link in chat. The headline: p50 is roughly 20% lower than the incumbent at our median prompt length, p95 delta is around 12% better, but p99 shows intermittent spikes that close the gap.

[01:05] Marcus: When you say spike, what's the absolute magnitude at p99? Are we talking 100 ms or 1 second?

[01:12] Priya: Good question. In our runs the p99 is around 1.8s for Redwood baseline config, incumbent sits at 2.1s in their published numbers, but we saw occasional 3.2s outliers correlated to batch flushes and cold KV cache misses.

[01:40] Ellen: Cold KV cache misses — is that from infrequently repeated prompts, or from leader eviction patterns?

[01:48] Priya: Likely both. Our KV heatmap shows lower cache hits for prompts that include long context vectors like user history. There's a small subset of requests that look like multi-shot sessions and those incur more KV misses which increases token generation times.

[02:12] Jordan: Right, and the other piece is batching policy. For throughput tests we used the continuous batching profile but with a tighter latency SLO, so sometimes the runtime flushes smaller batches to meet p50 targets which makes p99 worse. There's a trade-off.

[02:35] Rima: So what's the recommended knob here — increase batch size threshold or accept slightly higher p50 and reduce tails?

[02:42] Priya: For Solis' use case I'd suggest two parallel levers: 1) enable prefix-based KV caching for sessions we can identify, 2) slightly relax the max-latency cutoff so batches collect more, that reduces variance.

[03:05] Marcus: Do you have numbers showing the unit cost impact if we increase batch wait to hit larger batch sizes? Our finance team cares about tokens/second and GPU utilization.

[03:15] Priya: Yes, in the bench sheet there's a column 'tokens_per_gpu_hour' and estimated cost delta. Roughly speaking, moving batch_window from 8ms to 25ms increased throughput by ~18% and reduced per-token cost by about 11% in our simulated trace, but raised p95 by ~80ms in the median prompt.

[03:48] Ellen: That seems reasonable — we prefer predictable median latency for UX, but we can't have those 3s spikes during spikes in traffic.

[04:00] Jordan: We also ran a quantized variant (int8) that shaved CPU-GPU transfer time on our side. That helped throughput but introduced a slightly higher stochasticity in longer-form generations; quality regressions were measured on a small eval set, we can share the eval deck.

[04:24] Ellen: Was the quality delta significant? Our compliance folks are picky about hallucination rates.

[04:30] Priya: On the small set we saw a 0.5-1% BLEU-like metric drop for some prompt classes; not dramatic but worth validating on your prompt sets. We usually recommend running the quantized branch in non-critical paths first.

[04:50] Marcus: On the benchmark config — where are you running these? Hosted or Dedicated?

[04:55] Jordan: These Sprint 4 numbers were on Redwood hosted with routing pinned to our fastest region. We can reproduce on Dedicated or private VPC — that was part of the next-step proposal: short dedicated-slot canary so we can rule out noisy neighbors.

[05:18] Rima: If we do dedicated, what's the minimum reservation or window we need? Our infra team prefers short trials before committing.

[05:25] Priya: We can spin a short trial — we usually recommend a 2-hour window during low traffic where we allocate a single dedicated slot with the same model variant and measure p50/p95/p99 across your real traffic. It doesn't require long-term reservation for the trial.

[05:42] Ellen: That sounds good. Marcus, can you run the logs export? We need the 24h capture "anonymized" for Redwood to replay.

[05:50] Marcus: Yup I can do that. We'll scrub PII before sending. How do you want the traces formatted?

[05:56] Priya: CSV with timestamp, prompt_length_tokens, response_tokens, latency_ms, route_tag is perfect. If you can include a small sample of raw prompt text for quality eval (anonymized) that helps.

[06:12] Jordan: Quick note — the incumbent we were comparing against in the sheet is IncumbentCloudAI; we used their public SLA numbers and a few runs they shared earlier. There are some differences in cold start behavior — they did fine at p99 on synthetic bursts but worse on real session traces.

[06:35] Ellen: Our real traffic pattern has a heavy tail; about 6% of requests are multi-turn >1k tokens. Those are the ones that tend to blow up latency.

[06:45] Priya: In that case we should separate those into a routing carve-out: long-session requests can be routed to a higher-capacity slot or to an async workflow. Redwood supports routing policies that detect token-length and route accordingly.

[07:05] Marcus: We could also cache intermediate KV states for those sessions. How mature is your prefix KV caching?

[07:12] Priya: It's production-ready; we've seen ~40% reduction in token generation time for repeated multi-turn prompts when prefix caching is enabled and warmed. The tricky part is TTL and eviction — needs to align with your session semantics.

[07:30] Ellen: Can you share your eviction metrics and recommended TTL? We use fairly short sessions, typically under 15 minutes.

[07:37] Priya: For 15-minute sessions we recommend TTLs of 30 minutes to avoid churn; we'll provide the eviction curves in the bench sheet. Small memory cost but big latency upside.

[07:55] Jordan: Switching to throughput: we also did a sustained concurrency test at 250 RPS for 30 minutes. Redwood sustained 92% GPU utilization vs incumbent 83% in our config. That explains a lot of the cost delta.

[08:15] Marcus: At 250 RPS what's the average token-per-request in your sim? Our median is ~60 tokens, 95th is about 900.

[08:23] Priya: We used your supplied distribution — median 55, p95 860. We mirrored that distribution in the run.

[08:30] Jordan: One caveat — we had a transient where a garbage-collection-like cleanup on the host caused a 400ms jitter; we're investigating whether our kernel selection triggered a host-level process during compaction.

[08:45] Priya: We've instrumented those nodes and don't see an app-level GC, more like a device driver reset seen on rare kernels. We've already patched the runtime to avoid that in latest internal builds, but we'll reproduce in the canary.

[09:05] Ellen: Ok good. Those device-level resets are scary. If you can reproduce on our traces then we'll feel better to move to a trial.

[09:12] Marcus: How will we measure quality regressions during canary? We need automated checks to flag hallucinations or token-length regressions.

[09:22] Priya: We can wire a small eval harness that compares top-n completions and a simple entailment check for safety; it won't be a full human eval but will catch obvious regressions. We'll run it live during the 2-hour window and surface alerts.

[09:40] Rima: On security/compliance — if we do VPC peering for the canary, do you need access to our KMS? We prefer to keep keys within our account.

[09:49] Jordan: For a short canary we don't need your KMS. We can run under Redwood-managed keys for the trial and provide audit logs; if you move to production private deployment then we do KMS-integration and key-rotation protocols.

[10:05] Ellen: That helps. Send the SOC2 summary and audit log format please.

[10:10] Jordan: Will do. I'll attach the SOC2 summary and the RT log schema to the bench sheet.

[10:18] Priya: I want to highlight a small anomaly from the p95 chart — a cluster of requests at minute 22 in the run that had unusually high token counts and blocked batching. Looks like a scheduled background job in Solis' system that triggered a burst.

[10:32] Marcus: That's likely our daily analytics job. We usually run an ETL at 02:15 UTC that makes a batch of long prompts for training. Good catch.

[10:40] Priya: If we mask that traffic for the head-to-head comparison we get a cleaner signal — otherwise it skews p99. For production routing we can create a carve-out rule for the ETL traffic.

[10:52] Ellen: We'll coordinate to either move that job or tag it so you can filter it out.

[11:00] Jordan: Quick poll — are folks comfortable with the dedicated-slot trial on Jun 3, 02:00 UTC for 2 hours? Priya and I can be on-call for the run.

[11:10] Marcus: Jun 3 at 02:00 works for infra. Ellen ok?

[11:13] Ellen: Works for me. Rima is fine with the trial as long as we keep keys internal.

[11:20] Priya: Terrific. I'll size the dedicated slot for the trial: one slot with X GPUs (we propose 2xA100-v4 equiv) and config the batch window to 25ms for the test, and also run a control with 8ms to show tradeoffs.

[11:42] Marcus: Can you include the exact instance types so our network and budget teams can preliminarily sign off?

[11:48] Priya: Yes I'll include instance types and an estimated cost for the 2-hour window in the follow-up.

[12:00] Jordan: For the head-to-head we'll need a canonical prompt set — Priya will prepare a 500-sample set drawn from your trace, anonymized. We should freeze that set by Jun 2.

[12:12] Ellen: I'll review and flag any sensitive prompts. We can also toss in a few synthetic long sessions that mimic our worst-case.

[12:20] Priya: Great. On the bench sheet I'll also add a tab with p95/p99 per prompt-class so you can see which classes drive tails.

[12:40] Rima: One last governance question — if the canary shows better p50 but worse p99 for a class, what's your recommended rollout plan? We don't want to degrade customer experience mid-rollout.

[12:52] Jordan: We recommend canary + automatic fallback policy: do a canary at 5% of traffic, run live quality checks for 2 hours; if p99 > threshold or quality alerts fire, route back to incumbent. We can configure weighted rollouts and automatic rollback after n failures.

[13:15] Marcus: That fallback automation will be crucial. Can you share a sample rollback policy?

[13:22] Priya: I'll add a sample policy in the follow-up. It will include guard rails (p95 delta threshold, quality alert count) and a rollback playbook.

[13:40] Ellen: OK thanks. Any other open items?

[13:45] Jordan: Action items again: Redwood will share bench sheet + raw runs (due Jun 1), Solis will share 24h traces (due May 31), Priya to prepare canary sizing and playbook (due Jun 2), Marcus to confirm VPC/firewall and schedule the 2-hour window Jun 3 02:00 UTC.

[14:05] Rima: Sounds good. Thanks everyone, this was productive.

[14:12] Jordan: Thanks — we'll follow up in email and Slack with the links.

[14:18] [call ends]
